title: Huitzilopochtli: Birth and Battle
subtitle: A Mexica divine birth in Spence's account

birth.author: Lewis Spence
birth.locator: Chapter II · MEXICAN MYTHOLOGY; Chapter II · MEXICAN MYTHOLOGY, normalized characters 28562-29730
birth.excerpt: It recounts how, under the shadow of the mountain of Coatepec, near the Toltec city of Tollan, there dwelt a pious widow called Coatlicue, the mother of a tribe of Indians called Centzonuitznaua, who had a daughter called Coyolxauhqui, and who daily repaired to a small hill with the intention of offering up prayers to the gods in a penitent spirit of piety. Whilst occupied in her devotions one day she was surprised by a small ball of brilliantly coloured feathers falling upon her from on high. She was pleased by the bright variety of its hues, and placed it in her bosom, intending to offer it up to the sun-god. Some time afterwards she learnt that she was to become the mother of another child. Her sons, hearing of this, rained abuse upon her, being incited to humiliate her in every possible way by their sister Coyolxauhqui. Coatlicue went about in fear and anxiety; but the spirit of her unborn infant came and spoke to her and gave her words of encouragement, soothing her troubled heart. Her sons, however, were resolved to wipe out what they considered an insult to their race by the death of their mother, and took counsel with one another to slay her.
birth.note: Verbatim prose from Lewis Spence's early twentieth-century synthesis, not a direct translation of the Indigenous source material he discusses. Preserve its dated, colonial framing.

battle.author: Lewis Spence
battle.locator: Chapter II · MEXICAN MYTHOLOGY; Chapter II · MEXICAN MYTHOLOGY, normalized characters 31163-31544
battle.excerpt: He shattered Coyolxauhqui with a flash of serpentine lightning, and then gave chase to the Centzonuitznaua, whom he pursued four times round the mountain. They did not attempt to defend themselves, but fled incontinently. Many perished in the waters of the adjoining lake, to which they had rushed in their despair. All were slain save a few who escaped to a place called Uitzlampa

narrativeBlocks.title: A miraculous pregnancy
narrativeBlocks.body: At Coatepec hill, the mother-goddess Coatlicue is sweeping the shrine when a ball of feathers falls from the sky; she tucks it into her bosom and becomes pregnant — to the fury of her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her four hundred sons.

narrativeBlocks.title: Born fully armed
narrativeBlocks.body: As the siblings march up the hill to kill their mother for the disgrace, Huitzilopochtli is born fully grown and armed — hummingbird feathers, shield, and the fire-serpent Xiuhcoatl in his hand.

narrativeBlocks.title: The moon's defeat
narrativeBlocks.body: He strikes Coyolxauhqui and sends her tumbling down the hill in pieces — the Mexica read her dismemberment in the moon's phases, and the four hundred brothers became the stars.

narrativeBlocks.title: A war god's charter
narrativeBlocks.body: The myth is a charter: Huitzilopochtli is born fighting, the sun to his sister's moon — the patron of a people who built an empire on war.

narrativeBlocks.title: Theology at the capital
narrativeBlocks.body: At Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, the offerings to Huitzilopochtli faced Coyolxauhqui's great carved stone at the pyramid's foot — the myth was built into the city itself.
